summary: This informational document describes revisions to operational practices that separate the function of the arpa top-level domain in the DNS from its historical operation alongside the DNS root zone.

plainLanguage.summary: The arpa domain was run together with the main root of the name system for historical reasons. This document describes changes so the two are run separately.

questions: arpa and the dns root zone
why separate arpa from the dns root zone
subtitle: How the arpa domain gets its own nameserver names, separate from the DNS root servers.

tldr.problem: The arpa zone has been served directly by a subset of the root servers, which ties its management to the root zone and has caused some IETF proposals to be discarded.
tldr.mechanism: Give the arpa zone its own nameserver hostnames under ns.arpa (a.ns.arpa, b.ns.arpa and so on), initially pointing at the same addresses, and then work toward fully separate infrastructure and publication.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3172 and sets out the steps and end conditions for full technical separation of the arpa zone from the root zone.

today: RFC 9120 is an Informational IAB document that updates RFC 3172. The unit metadata shows nothing obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why arpa Needs Separating
sections.content:
The arpa top-level domain is designated an infrastructure domain that supports techniques defined by Internet standards. Zones under it provide mappings such as IP addresses to domain names and E.164 numbers to URIs, and it also holds special-use names such as home.

Historically, arpa has been served on almost all of the root nameservers, and RFC 3172 envisaged that the operational requirements for the root servers would apply to the arpa servers. This bundling entwined the management of the two zones, and some IETF proposals involving arpa were discarded because of the risk of conflict with operations on the root zone or root servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things that live in the same building cannot change their doors or walls without bothering each other. Moving them apart lets each one change what it needs.

sections.title: Requirements That Stay the Same
sections.content:
This change does not weaken the operational requirements of RFC 3172. Future requirements for arpa are encouraged to follow strong baselines such as those in RFC 7720.

Other zones delegated within arpa are untouched. For example, ip6.arpa continues to be managed under RFC 5855.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for keeping arpa safe and reliable stay just as strict. Only where it lives changes.

sections.title: The Transition Process
sections.content:
First, new hostnames are dedicated to the arpa servers: a new namespace ns.arpa, with the nameserver set labelled a.ns.arpa, b.ns.arpa, c.ns.arpa and so on. The zone initially maps these names to the same IP addresses that already serve it under root-servers.net, so the underlying hosts do not change. Because these nameservers sit completely within arpa, they need glue records in the root zone, which matches current practice.

Later phases could use new hosts to replace or augment the root nameserver hosts, and separate the editing and distribution of the arpa zone from the root zone. Any change of parties providing the service is treated as normal management under RFC 3172.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one is only a change of names on the mailboxes. The same mail carriers deliver to the same addresses, so nothing breaks while the move is prepared.

sections.title: When Separation Is Complete
sections.content:
Full technical separation minimally requires three things:

  • The arpa zone shares no hostnames in its nameserver set with the root zone.
  • The hosts serving arpa are not the root nameservers, share no IPv4 or IPv6 addresses with them, and are provisioned separately.
  • The editorial and publication process for arpa has no common dependencies with the root zone process.

The goal is to allow novel uses of arpa without the risk of impacting root zone and root server operations. The RFC recognizes that this needs a deliberative process with significant coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving is finished when arpa has its own names, its own machines and its own way of publishing changes.

sections.title: IANA Actions and Security
sections.content:
IANA is to coordinate creation of the ns.arpa namespace and fill it with address records matching the contemporary root servers in root-servers.net. It may be set up directly in the arpa zone as an empty nonterminal or as a dedicated ns.arpa zone. IANA will initially migrate the 12 NS records for the arpa zone to the new entries. Afterwards the IAB and IANA will consult with relevant parties on reducing reliance on the root zone and root servers.

On security, the RFC says the security of the arpa zone is not necessarily affected by these changes, and that robust practices for administering and distributing the zone, including signing it with DNSSEC, remain necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA is asked to set up the new names and copy the old addresses into them. Keeping the zone signed and well looked after stays important.

items.title: Own hostnames
items.text: No shared names in the nameserver set.

items.title: Own hosts
items.text: Different machines and no shared IPv4 or IPv6 addresses.

items.title: Own publication
items.text: No common dependency with the root zone process.
